ideas.rule: When a file is relocated into an artifact type with different frontmatter requirements (command -> skill, rule -> skill), the conversion must add the fields the destination type requires; a rename alone is not a conversion.
ideas.why: Git renders these as 100%-similarity renames, so both human review and any diff-line-scoped checker see almost nothing changed, while 14 artifacts silently become non-loadable. No current check keys on the artifact type changing across a rename.

ideas.rule: When a change introduces a frontmatter block into an artifact that previously had none, the block must be complete on arrival — a partial manifest is worse than no manifest, because parsers that tolerated a bare-body file will now validate the block and reject or silently drop the skill.
ideas.why: SK02 already requires `name` and `description`, but it is written as a steady-state property of a file. Nothing in the checklist distinguishes 'this file has always lacked frontmatter' (a standing condition, correctly suppressed) from 'this diff added frontmatter and left it incomplete' (a fresh, high-signal defect). The transition is the checkable moment and the one a reviewer should be pushed to catch.

ideas.rule: A script invoked by a skill must live under that skill's own `scripts/` directory. A `scripts/` folder placed directly in the skills root is not part of any skill, is indistinguishable from a malformed skill missing its SKILL.md, and cannot be installed or vendored with the skill that uses it.
ideas.why: skill-script-checklist.md is a stub, and spec-conformant-layout-SK15 only governs the interior of a single skill directory — neither can see a script parked as a sibling of the skills. This PR moved a script from `.claude/scripts/` into `.claude/skills/scripts/`, i.e. into a pseudo-skill directory, and no check in the catalog can flag it. The pattern generalizes: any repo with scripts shared across skills faces the same choice.

ideas.rule: A skill script's usage/help text must state the path from which it is meant to be invoked, and that path must match where the skill's body tells the agent to run it — otherwise a move updates one and silently leaves the other stale.
ideas.why: Nothing checks consistency between a script's self-documented invocation path and the callers in SKILL.md bodies. This PR had to hand-edit the same path in four places across three files to stay correct; a check comparing the two would catch the common case where one is missed. no-broken-links-SK13 does not cover it because it validates paths *named by* a skill, not paths a script asserts about itself.

ideas.rule: A skill whose frontmatter sets `disable-model-invocation: true` should be graded against a different description standard than a model-invocable one: its description is a human picker label, not a routing signal, so trigger-phrase requirements should be relaxed while clarity-of-effect requirements tighten.
ideas.why: skill-checklist.md's SK05 and SK08 both assume the description drives model selection. For the 9 skills in this diff that disable model invocation, that assumption is false, and applying SK05 literally produces findings a maintainer would correctly reject. A checklist that branches on `disable-model-invocation` would keep both checks meaningful instead of forcing reviewers to guess.

ideas.rule: Before adding a subagent, confirm no existing skill already owns its domain; if one does, the subagent must either delegate to that skill or state which artifact wins on conflict.
ideas.why: subagent-checklist.md is a stub, so nothing catches a subagent silently duplicating a skill. The standards checklist has exactly this check as not-shadowed-by-skill-SD03; subagents need the equivalent, and this PR is a clean instance — a `reviewer` subagent and a `review` skill now cover the same ground with no stated precedence.

ideas.rule: A subagent's frontmatter must declare its tool grant explicitly and minimally, and the grant must match the work described in its body — the subagent equivalent of least-privilege-SK22.
ideas.why: subagent-checklist.md has no checks at all, so a subagent can request broad tools with no scrutiny. Here `tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash` grants arbitrary shell to an agent whose stated job is read-only diff review; nothing in the current catalog can flag that, because SK22 is scoped to skills and keys off `allowed-tools`.

ideas.rule: A subagent must define its output contract — what it returns, in what shape, and what it emits when it finds nothing — since the parent agent consumes the output programmatically.
ideas.why: This is the single most consequential subagent property and no check exists for it. Worth codifying as a positive check because it is mechanically verifiable and generalizes to every repo; reviewer.md happens to do it well (a numbered Return block including the empty case), which makes it a good reference example rather than a violation.

ideas.rule: A harness config that registers an agent or capability by file path must point at a path that exists, and the path's base directory must be unambiguous (relative to the config file vs. the repo root).
ideas.why: other-checklist.md is a stub, so nothing validates harness-config references the way no-broken-links-SK13 validates skill links. `.codex/config.toml` declares `config_file = "agents/reviewer.toml"` — resolvable only if read relative to `.codex/`, which the file never states. A path-resolution check would generalize to every settings/mcp file in the benchmark.

ideas.rule: A script shipped with a skill must not name its own path in usage/help text; when it does, that path must resolve after any move, and the check should fail if the literal path string in the script does not match the script's actual location.
ideas.why: skill-script-checklist.md is a stub, so nothing catches the single most common script defect: a rename that updates the SKILL.md pointer but leaves the script's embedded self-reference stale. Mechanically checkable in any repo — grep the script for its own basename and compare the surrounding path to its real location.

ideas.rule: A skill script must live under the skill's `scripts/` subfolder, carry the executable bit, and open with a valid shebang.
ideas.why: The skill checklist's SK15 covers layout for the skill as a container, but there is no script-side check that a helper is actually runnable as invoked. This script happens to be `0755` with `#!/bin/bash`, but nothing in the current checklists would have noticed if it weren't.

ideas.rule: An artifact must not instruct the agent to weaken host or container security posture (world-writable permissions on a privileged socket, disabling TLS verification, `--no-sandbox`, blanket `sudo`) without stating the blast radius and an environment precondition that bounds it.
ideas.why: SK21 covers outright injection, exfiltration and remote-exec, but has no clause for advice that quietly degrades the security of the machine the agent runs on. `sudo chmod 666 /var/run/docker.sock` grants every local process root-equivalent control of the Docker daemon; it is given here as an unconditional recovery step with no note that it is acceptable only inside a disposable cloud VM. This pattern recurs across dev-environment skills in many repos and is mechanically greppable.

ideas.rule: A skill that documents environment or service setup must state how to verify each step succeeded, not only the command to run.
ideas.why: Setup skills are the artifact class most likely to be executed blind by an agent, and a step that silently half-fails (daemon up but socket unreachable, migrations applied against the wrong env file) produces a long, confusing failure much later. Nothing in skill-checklist.md requires verification criteria outside the Workflows section, which by its own preamble applies only to multi-step workflow skills, not to a setup reference like this one. SK17 is the nearest check and it explicitly does not reach here.

ideas.rule: A skill that sets `disable-model-invocation: true` must still declare `allowed-tools`, and its description should be written for a human picking it from a list rather than for a model matching triggers.
ideas.why: Disabling model invocation changes how a skill is *selected* but not what it is permitted to *do*, and the current checklist gives no signal that the two frontmatter fields are independent. Reviewers (including this one) reach for the argument that trigger phrasing stops mattering once invocation is manual, which is half true and needs settling once in the checklist rather than re-litigated per PR. Mechanically checkable and applies to every harness that supports the field.

ideas.rule: A skill whose process embeds a shell command with hardcoded flags against an external CLI should state the command's contract (what it returns, what to do when it returns nothing) rather than only the invocation.
ideas.why: skill-checklist SK17 asks for completion criteria on workflow skills but nothing checks that an embedded command is *usable* — a hardcoded `--limit 30` silently defines the review window, and the skill never says what to do if the window contains no user-facing change even though its own principles anticipate exactly that case. This generalises to any skill that wraps a CLI, which is most automation skills.

ideas.rule: A skill that documents a code API surface (helper functions, exported utilities) should link to the source module rather than restate the signature list inline, since the inline list silently drifts from the code.
ideas.why: SK14 covers stale model names and absolute paths but nothing covers an advice file mirroring a real module's API. The 'Eval utilities' list added here (describeEvalMatrix / evalReporter.record / judgeBinary / judgeMultiple / CRITERIA.*) is a verbatim mirror of apps/web/__tests__/eval/*, and a later PR (2210-era refactor to createEvalReporter()) did in fact leave one copy stale.

ideas.rule: A guideline that prohibits a specific library API must name the sanctioned alternative, or the agent is left with a dead end and will invent one.
ideas.why: GR06 only nudges toward scoped phrasing and GR03 only bounds length; neither requires a prohibition to be actionable. A ban on `prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => ...)` with no replacement (sequential writes? `$transaction([...])` array form? application-level idempotency?) is the most common failure mode of one-line rule additions and would fire in any repo.

ideas.rule: When a skill is deleted or emptied, its guidance must land in exactly one destination — a check should flag content that is deleted from one artifact and simultaneously added to two or more others in the same diff.
ideas.why: Consolidation PRs are where duplication is born: the author fans one skill's content out to a reference doc *and* a context file *and* a sibling skill, and each copy looks locally reasonable. GR01 catches the resulting duplicate only if a reviewer happens to compare two added files against each other. A same-diff fan-out check is mechanically detectable from the patch alone and generalises to every repo that reorganises its artifacts.

ideas.rule: A `SKILL.md` reduced to a single pointer line should reference a file inside its own bundle; a pointer that crosses into another skill's directory is a sign the two skills should be merged or the target promoted to a shared standards doc.
ideas.why: Nothing today grades cross-skill pointers. Here `e2e/SKILL.md` and `llm-test/SKILL.md` each become a one-line "Read and follow `.claude/skills/testing/<x>.md`" — the skills survive only as trigger stubs whose content lives in a third skill's directory, so SK10's "references stay one level deep" is satisfied by letter while the bundle boundary is broken. Detectable by checking whether a referenced path stays under the skill's own root.

ideas.rule: A line moved into `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` from a deleted skill should be graded against the context file's budget as an addition, and the check should ask whether it is repo-wide enough to deserve always-loaded status.
ideas.why: CF01 measures only total size, so a context file absorbs orphaned guidance one line at a time and never trips a threshold until it is far too late. This PR moves three lines up from two deleted skills; each is individually defensible, and the aggregate ratchet is invisible to every current check. Applies to any repo that consolidates tooling into a context file.

ideas.rule: A subagent definition must have at least one live invocation path — a context file, skill, command, or harness config that tells an agent when to call it. Removing the last reference to a subagent should either delete the subagent or state what now invokes it.
ideas.why: subagent-checklist.md is a stub, so nothing today catches an orphaned subagent. This PR deleted the only prose that ever told an agent to invoke `.claude/agents/reviewer.md`; the file (and its .codex/agents/reviewer.toml mirror, registered in .codex/config.toml) remains in the tree with no remaining caller in AGENTS.md, any SKILL.md, or any rule. An unreachable subagent is dead weight that still costs discovery attention and silently rots. The check generalizes: it is the subagent analogue of skill-checklist's no-broken-links, and would fire on any repo where an agent definition is stranded.

ideas.rule: A skill that instructs the agent to mutate the developer's local environment — flipping feature flags, symlinking or creating `.env` files, installing dependencies, starting long-lived background processes — must state how that state is restored or torn down afterwards.
ideas.why: The skill checklist covers least privilege via `allowed-tools` (SK22) and injection/exfil (SK21), but nothing checks that side effects on the developer's machine are reversible. A skill that enables a feature flag "so the test passes" and never turns it off leaves the repo in a changed state that the next agent run inherits silently. Mechanically detectable: setup instructions with no matching teardown section.

ideas.rule: A shell procedure in an artifact must not hardcode a platform-specific absolute binary path without stating the OS assumption or deriving the path.
ideas.why: skill-checklist SK14 forbids 'absolute user paths' but says nothing about absolute *system* paths, so a macOS-only invocation passes every existing check and then fails silently for any contributor on Linux or Windows — the agent runs it, gets 'no such file', and has no instruction telling it the step was platform-gated. Mechanically checkable (`/Applications/`, `/usr/local/opt/`, `C:\Program Files\`) and applies to any repo with mixed-OS contributors.

ideas.rule: A skill that can perform destructive or irreversible remote mutations should set `disable-model-invocation: true` (or an equivalent explicit-invocation gate), not merely describe the mutation carefully.
ideas.why: SK22 ties the side-effect gate to deploy/commit/send verbs and only bites when `allowed-tools` is present. This skill's description invites implicit model invocation and its documented surface includes `rules delete` and a full-replacement `rules update` against a user's live production account — exactly the case the gate exists for, yet nothing currently fires. Generalises to any skill wrapping a write-capable API client.

ideas.rule: A per-harness sidecar that grants an agent permission (e.g. `allow_implicit_invocation: true`) must be justified against the skill's own invocation gate, and the two must not disagree.
ideas.why: other-checklist.md is a stub, so nothing grades a policy sidecar at all. Here `agents/openai.yaml` sets `allow_implicit_invocation: true` for a skill that can delete rules, and no check compares that grant against the skill's own frontmatter. Any repo shipping multi-harness sidecars can end up with one harness silently more permissive than another.

ideas.rule: A skill's `metadata` frontmatter should not be a single-line inline JSON blob; structured YAML keeps it diffable and reviewable.
ideas.why: SK02 checks only that optional fields are spec-conformant, not that they are legible. The 400-character one-line `metadata:` value here encodes install steps, required binaries and required env vars — real security-relevant configuration that is effectively unreviewable in a diff. Mechanically checkable (frontmatter value length / inline-JSON detection) and applies to any packaged skill.

ideas.rule: A guideline that names a concrete source path plus an in-code identifier (e.g. "bump `DRAFT_PIPELINE_VERSION` in `apps/web/utils/ai/reply/draft-attribution.ts`") should be flagged as fragile — the advice silently goes stale when the file is moved or the constant renamed, and nothing in the repo links the two.
ideas.why: The guideline checklist covers duplication, conciseness, home, force and phrasing, but nothing checks whether advice is coupled to a code location that can move without the artifact being updated. This is a mechanically checkable condition (does the cited path still exist? does the identifier still appear in it?) and would fire in any repo whose artifacts reference implementation details.

ideas.rule: When a skill's body names a specific tool it must call by name (e.g. `CronCreate`, `TodoWrite`, an MCP tool), that tool must appear in the skill's `allowed-tools`, and vice versa — the manifest and the body must agree.
ideas.why: SK22 (least-privilege) only fires when `allowed-tools` exists, so a skill that hard-depends on a named tool and declares nothing at all passes every current check. The failure mode is silent: the skill runs in a harness where that tool is unavailable and the step is skipped rather than erroring. A body-vs-manifest cross-check is mechanically decidable and would fire on skills in any repo.

ideas.rule: A skill that starts a background, recurring, or long-running process must state its stop condition and how the user cancels it.
ideas.why: Nothing in skill-checklist.md covers lifecycle of side-effecting background work. pr-watch does state a self-cancel condition inside its embedded prompt, which is the good case — but only by luck, and there is no check that would have caught its absence. Any skill that spawns a loop, cron, watcher, or daemon has the same requirement, so this generalises well beyond this repo.

ideas.rule: A named list of environment-specific identifiers (CI check names, bot logins, service names) embedded in an instruction should be marked as illustrative or sourced from the repo, not hard-coded as the closed set the agent matches against.
ideas.why: Advice like 'verify no reviewer checks (e.g. "Baz Reviewer", "cubic · AI code reviewer") are pending' silently stops working when a check is renamed or a new reviewer bot is added, and nothing fails loudly. This is a generic staleness class across skills and context files, and no current check covers it — SK14 covers stale model names only.

ideas.rule: When one skill delegates to another (invoking it by name or slash command), shared procedure — the commands to run, the exit conditions to check — must live in exactly one of them, with the other referencing it. Two skills in the same harness that restate each other's steps are a sync hazard, unlike deliberate cross-harness mirrors.
ideas.why: guideline-rule-checklist.md's GR01 catches a duplicated line but has no notion of *which* copy is canonical, and skill-checklist.md's SK27 only polices SKILL.md-vs-reference placement inside a single skill. Nothing checks the intra-harness skill-to-skill case, which is where this repo's pr-loop / pr-watch / address-pr-comments trio actually drifts. A check would need to distinguish it from the cross-harness duplication (.claude vs .codex) that repositories deliberately maintain.

ideas.rule: A subagent that exists to front an installed skill should delegate to it, not paraphrase its workflow; if the subagent restates more than a one-line trigger, flag it.
ideas.why: subagent-checklist.md is a stub, so nothing catches the most common subagent defect: a thin wrapper that copies the skill's steps and then also links the skill, guaranteeing two divergent copies of the same procedure. Generalizes to any repo pairing agents with skills.

ideas.rule: A subagent file must declare its tool access explicitly, the same way skill-checklist SK03 requires it of skills.
ideas.why: The new agent's frontmatter carries only `name` and `description` while the agent's whole purpose is shelling out to a CLI that mutates production email rules. A subagent with unbounded implicit tool access and side-effecting behavior is the exact case SK03/SK22 were written for on the skill side, and the stub subagent checklist has no analogue.

ideas.rule: When a skill is exposed at more than one discovery path (symlink, mirrored directory, packaging manifest), exactly one path must be canonical and the others must not be independently editable.
ideas.why: This PR adds `skills/inbox-zero-api` as a symlink to `clawhub/inbox-zero-api` purely so Cursor's `skills/*/SKILL.md` discovery finds it, and documents the canonicality rule in prose in clawhub/README.md. Nothing in the catalog checks that multi-path exposure is a link rather than a copy — the failure mode (two real directories that silently diverge) is common in repos serving several harnesses.

ideas.rule: A harness plugin/packaging manifest that declares a version must be checked against the artifacts it packages, or the version pins nothing.
ideas.why: other-checklist.md is a stub. `.cursor-plugin/plugin.json` declares `"version": "1.0.0"` while the skill it packages carries no version field at all (repo-wide house style), so the manifest version is decorative and gives installers no way to tell what they received.

ideas.rule: A path an artifact tells the agent to read must resolve from a checkout — not point into `node_modules/`, a build output, or another install- or version-generated directory whose existence and contents are outside the repo's control.
ideas.why: skill-checklist SK13 validates relative paths but only inside a skill directory, and context-file-checklist has no path-validity check at all. A pointer into a dependency's internals is uniquely bad: it silently stops resolving on the next dependency bump, and the agent then either reads nothing or reads docs for the wrong version — exactly the failure the instruction was written to prevent. This would fire on artifacts in any repo and is mechanically checkable.

ideas.rule: A rule file whose frontmatter has an empty `description:`, empty `globs:`, and `alwaysApply: false` can never be selected by the harness — flag it as inert rather than as a style nit.
ideas.why: rule-checklist.md grades only the body's content, not whether the file can ever load. A 120-line rule that no glob or description will ever match is pure dead weight in the repo, and the defect is mechanically detectable from frontmatter alone. This would fire in any Cursor-using repo where the scaffold default was left in place.

ideas.rule: A skill that documents CLI-style flags should state each flag's default value or the fallback behaviour when it is absent, in the same place the flag is listed.
ideas.why: No current check asks whether an argument-taking skill defines its no-argument behaviour. Here the fallback was only added retroactively for `--base-url`; `--max-parallel` and `--group` in the same usage block still have no stated default, so the agent has to guess. This is mechanically checkable (every flag listed in a usage block should have a documented default or an explicit ask-the-user path) and would fire on command/skill artifacts in any repo.

ideas.rule: A vendored skill installed from an upstream project must be marked as vendored inside the artifact itself (e.g. a `source`/`upstream` frontmatter field or a header line naming the origin and pinned revision), not only in an external lockfile.
ideas.why: Nothing in skill-checklist.md distinguishes authored from vendored content. Without an in-file marker, a reviewer (human or agent) cannot tell that edits to `.claude/skills/agent-browser/SKILL.md` will be silently overwritten on the next vendor sync, and review effort is spent on a file nobody in the repo can fix. The provenance here lives only in `skills-lock.json`, a file that is never opened during a skill review.

ideas.rule: A skill directory must not introduce top-level subfolders outside the spec set (`references/`, `scripts/`, `assets/`, `evals/`); shipped shell examples belong in `scripts/` or `assets/`.
ideas.why: SK15 already covers this for authored skills, but the recurring real-world offender is a `templates/` folder — seen here and worth calling out explicitly, since 'templates' reads as legitimate to authors and silently breaks tooling that walks the spec folders. Recorded as an idea rather than a finding because this instance is vendored and therefore not actionable by this repo.

ideas.rule: A skill whose body is a set of shell commands with placeholder arguments must state how the placeholder is resolved before the first command that uses it, not after.
ideas.why: skill-checklist.md checks structure, links and layout but has no check on the internal ordering of a procedural body. Here the two `gh pr edit <PR_NUMBER>` snippets appear at lines 8-14 and the instruction for how to obtain <PR_NUMBER> only at lines 24-28, so an agent reading top-down reaches an executable command with an unresolved placeholder first. This failure mode is generic across command-style skills in any repo and is mechanically checkable: a placeholder appearing in a fenced command block before its resolution step.

ideas.rule: A skill whose body reduces to a single command invocation with no branching, no preconditions, and no failure handling should be questioned: it adds a routing hop and a description to match against without carrying knowledge the agent lacks.
ideas.why: The skill checklist grades whether a SKILL.md is too fat (SK09, SK10, SK27) but has no check for the opposite failure — a skill so thin it does not justify existing as a separate discoverable artifact. Simplification PRs like this one can overshoot, and the resulting near-empty skill still consumes description-matching budget on every turn. Mechanically checkable (body under ~N tokens with no reference docs, no scripts, and no conditional logic) and applicable to any repo with a skill directory.

ideas.rule: When a change removes instructions from an artifact, the remaining text must not leave a documented capability unreachable — check that every operation the skill's description promises still has a stated invocation.
ideas.why: Deletion-only artifact PRs are reviewed far less carefully than additions, yet they are where capability silently disappears. Here the removal took out the `--remove-label` command and the `gh pr view --json number --jq '.number'` lookup that let the agent act on "label the current PR", which is the most likely way a user phrases the request. No checklist covers coverage regressions in a shrinking artifact. Generalizes to any artifact type.

ideas.rule: A guideline that names a shell command must be resolvable from the working directory the surrounding document implies — verify the script exists in the manifest for that directory, or state the directory explicitly.
ideas.why: Command advice is the highest-traffic content in testing/build skills and it rots silently: the package script gets renamed or moved between workspace and root and the prose keeps working syntactically while failing in practice. Mechanically checkable in any repo with a package manifest, and no current GR or SK check covers factual resolvability of a named command.

ideas.rule: When a skill's SKILL.md carries a quick-reference command block that a reference doc also documents, the SKILL.md form must be the canonical one and the reference must not restate a divergent variant.
ideas.why: Skills routinely keep a cheat-sheet in SKILL.md plus a fuller reference doc, and the two drift. SK27 covers 'detail lives in a reference doc' but nothing checks that the summary and the detail agree. PR 2598 in this same repo is a fix PR whose entire purpose was repairing exactly this drift.

ideas.rule: Advice that mirrors a third-party package's API surface (endpoint lists, config schemas, version-specific defaults) must either link to the upstream doc or state how it stays in sync — an inlined copy has no owner and drifts silently.
ideas.why: Neither GR01 (which searches only in-repo containers) nor GR04 squarely covers duplication of an *external* doc, yet this is one of the most common ways an agent-facing guideline file rots. GR01's scope is explicitly in-repo, so the check that should have fired here doesn't exist.

ideas.rule: A guideline that names a package script (`pnpm <script>`, `npm run <script>`) must reference a script that actually exists in the relevant `package.json`.
ideas.why: Context files and skills accumulate command references that silently rot when scripts are renamed or removed, and the agent then burns a turn on a failing command before recovering. This is fully mechanical — resolve the workspace filter, read its `package.json` scripts map — and applies to every JS/TS repo, with direct analogues in Make, Just, Taskfile, and Cargo. Nothing in the context-file or guideline checklists checks command validity; `no-broken-links-SK13` covers only relative file paths, and only for skills.

ideas.rule: Advice that hardcodes a model identifier, SDK version, or other externally-versioned name must be flagged: it goes stale silently and has to be updated in every copy.
ideas.why: skill-checklist SK14 catches 'stale model names' but only inside a SKILL.md container; skill reference docs and standards docs are graded by the GR checklist, which has no equivalent check. This PR exists solely to chase a model rename through a doc example, and it had to touch both the doc and the source catalog — exactly the maintenance tax the check would surface. Mechanically detectable (regex over known model-name shapes) and applies to any repo whose artifacts document model choices.

ideas.rule: A skill's ancillary markdown files should live under references/ rather than the skill root, so the root stays SKILL.md plus the four spec subfolders.
ideas.why: SK15 already states this, but it fires as a container finding on the SKILL.md, which means a PR that only edits one of the stray root files (as this one does) produces nothing — the layout defect is invisible from the diff that touches it. Worth a check that attributes the layout problem to any file in the skill, not only SKILL.md.

ideas.rule: An advice line that hard-codes a specific dependency version, model name, or other fast-moving literal must either point at the file that owns that value or be marked as time-sensitive, because nothing will re-check it when the constraint expires.
ideas.why: skill-checklist SK14 covers 'stale model names' and 'unmarked time-sensitive claims' as a container-level structural check, but the guideline checklist has no per-line equivalent — so a single advice line pinning `4.1.0` against `zod@3.25.76` passes every GR check on its own terms. Version-pin rot is one of the most common ways artifact advice silently becomes wrong, and it is mechanically detectable (semver literals in prose). This would fire in any repo.

ideas.rule: A line edited inside a fenced or indented code block must preserve the block's indentation and delimiters; check that the edited region still parses as the same block.
ideas.why: Search-and-replace refactors across artifact docs routinely strip leading whitespace, silently breaking an indented code block so the agent copies malformed content or reads prose as code. Nothing in the skill or guideline checklists covers structural integrity of reference-doc code samples — SK14 covers unclosed fences in SKILL.md only, and reference docs are graded by the guideline checklist, which has no structural check at all. This is mechanically checkable and would fire in any repo.

ideas.rule: A skill whose workflow performs irreversible VCS operations (branch reset, force-checkout, push) must state the recovery path or precondition for each — e.g. what happens if the branch has unpushed local work.
ideas.why: `git checkout -B <branch> origin/main` silently discards any prior state on that branch. Workflow skills that automate git are increasingly common and no current check asks whether a destructive step is guarded. Applies to any repo with an automation skill.

ideas.rule: A per-harness sidecar manifest shipped alongside an artifact (openai.yaml, agent.toml, plugin.json) must not restate identity fields the primary artifact already declares, and where it does, the values must match.
ideas.why: other-checklist.md is a stub, so nothing catches a sidecar whose `display_name`/`short_description` silently diverges from the SKILL.md `name`/`description` after an edit to one and not the other. Multi-harness repos accumulate these sidecars fast and the drift is invisible in review. Mechanically checkable and applies to any repo running more than one harness.

ideas.rule: A skill whose body names repo-specific source paths should say what to do when those paths do not resolve, rather than presenting them as the definitive location.
ideas.why: This skill hard-codes four `apps/web/utils/ai/**`-style globs as where prompts live. Directory moves are routine and the skill has no fallback, so it degrades into scanning nothing without any signal. Generic across skills that embed repo topology; SK13 only checks links inside the skill directory, not paths into the host repo.

ideas.rule: When a skill's body grows an instruction outside the scope its `description` declares, either the instruction or the description must change — frontmatter scope and body scope must stay in sync.
ideas.why: SK05 checks that a description is actionable and SK07 that it is honest at the time of writing, but neither re-checks the description against the body as the body accretes. Scope drift by append is the dominant decay mode for long-lived skills: `create-pr`'s description still says 'Commit changes and open a pull request with safe metadata' while the body now also mandates a performance analysis. This is checkable on any skill diff that adds a body instruction without touching the description.

ideas.rule: When an artifact instructs the agent to download an executable from the network and run it, the instruction must pin an exact version and provide an integrity check (checksum or signature) alongside the URL.
ideas.why: skill-checklist SK21 only catches the blatant `curl … | sh` shape, so a two-step download-then-chmod+x — which has identical trust properties — passes cleanly. Pinning without verification still leaves the agent executing whatever that URL serves at run time. This is mechanically checkable (a fetch of a binary followed by an exec-enabling step, with no hash nearby) and would fire on setup/bootstrap skills in any repository.

ideas.rule: An artifact must not present credential-shaped assignments as a copyable block without marking them non-secret; placeholder or emulator credentials should be visibly labelled as such.
ideas.why: Nothing in the current checklists distinguishes a real leaked secret (SK21, error) from a deliberately fake one, so reviewers must judge case by case and the check gives no credit for labelling. A rule requiring the block itself to carry the marker makes both the reviewer's and the agent's job mechanical, and generalises to any repo that documents local-dev credentials.

ideas.rule: A subagent or agent config must not hard-pin a provider model identifier without a stated review trigger or a fallback; a bare `model = "<vendor-model-id>"` line goes stale silently and is edited only by accident.
ideas.why: `subagent-checklist.md` is a stub, so nothing catches this today. This PR is itself the evidence: its only change to `.codex/agents/reviewer.toml` is bumping `model = "gpt-5.3-codex"` to `model = "gpt-5.5"`, a maintenance edit that must now be repeated by hand in every agent file on every model release, and the new `code-simplifier.toml` adds a third place to forget. Mechanically checkable across repos by matching known vendor model-id patterns in agent config.

ideas.rule: A subagent's instructions must not assert its own invocation policy ("operate autonomously and proactively", "run immediately after every change") — dispatch is the harness's decision, declared in config, not something the agent can grant itself.
ideas.why: This is the subagent analogue of SK07's 'always use first' trigger-hijacking clause, and `subagent-checklist.md` is a stub so nothing covers it. An agent body that claims proactive self-invocation either contradicts the dispatch config or, worse, causes the model to fire it unprompted; either way the real policy becomes unreadable from the config alone. Greppable and general.

ideas.rule: When a harness config registers a delegated agent, its `description` must be the routing signal for that agent and must not diverge from the description in the agent file it points at.
ideas.why: `other-checklist.md` is a stub. `.codex/config.toml` carries a per-agent `description` that the dispatcher matches on, entirely separate from the prose inside the referenced `.toml` — two descriptions for one agent, with nothing keeping them aligned. A drift check between a registry entry and its target artifact generalizes to any harness with an agent or skill registry.

ideas.rule: When the same guidance is mirrored across harnesses by design, exactly one copy must be the source and the others must be generated or explicitly marked as mirrors — a hand-maintained duplicate needs a marker naming its source of truth.
ideas.why: GR01 rejects duplication outright, which is the wrong answer for repos that legitimately run several harnesses; there is currently no check for the correct middle position. Here `.claude/skills/code-simplifier/SKILL.md` and `.codex/agents/code-simplifier.toml` were added in one commit saying substantially the same thing in two formats, already differing in detail (the TOML mentions path aliases and React component patterns; the Markdown does not), with nothing in either file naming the other. That divergence-on-day-one is the failure mode a mirror-marker check would catch.

ideas.rule: A context file that names a specific artifact as the authority for a topic must not also restate that topic's operational detail inline.
ideas.why: CF05 covers deferring to a *standards doc*, but the common modern case is a context file that both points at a skill and duplicates its content — the pointer exists, so the duplication is pure maintenance debt. This PR is direct evidence: one script rename forced a four-file synchronized edit. Generalizes to any repo with both a context file and skills.

ideas.rule: A skill reference doc that documents a configuration surface (env vars, CLI flags, config keys) should carry each key's contract in exactly one place — either an inline prose section or a consolidated table, not both.
ideas.why: guideline-rule-checklist.md's GR01 is aimed at cross-file duplication of *instructions*; nothing in the skill or guideline checklists catches a reference doc that documents the same configuration key twice within itself, which is where defaults silently drift. This PR added three such double-documented keys in one diff.

ideas.rule: A guideline that states a preferred API plus an exception should present them as separate, labelled clauses (or a two-row do/don't pair), not as consecutive sentences in one paragraph.
ideas.why: GR03 catches padding and over-length but has nothing to say about *shape*. The recurring real-world defect is a rule whose exception is buried mid-paragraph, which models follow inconsistently. A structural check ("if a guideline contains a contrastive connective — but/except/keep/unless — split it") is mechanically checkable and would fire across every repo in the benchmark.

ideas.rule: A skill reference doc that documents a CLI entry point should name the package script or file that implements it, so a renamed script surfaces as a stale reference instead of silently mis-instructing the agent.
ideas.why: skill-checklist SK13 only validates relative paths inside the skill directory. Command/script names an artifact tells the agent to run are the more common staleness vector and nothing checks them. Here `pnpm --filter inbox-zero-ai eval-report` is asserted with no pointer back to the script it maps to.

ideas.rule: A harness settings/env file must declare the schema it validates against (`$schema`, or the harness's equivalent) when the harness publishes one.
ideas.why: other-checklist.md is a stub, so nothing today catches a settings file that silently accepts typo'd or dead keys. A `$schema` line is mechanically checkable, costs one line, and turns a whole class of silent misconfiguration into an editor-time error. This PR happens to do it right, which is what makes it a good template for a check that would fire on the many settings files that do not.

ideas.rule: When a harness settings file supports a per-developer local override (`*.local.*`), the override path must be git-ignored in the same change that introduces the shared file.
ideas.why: A committed local-override file leaks one developer's machine paths and, worse, silently overrides the shared config for everyone who pulls it. The check is mechanical: for any settings artifact whose harness documents a `.local` sibling, assert the sibling matches a `.gitignore` entry. Nothing in the current checklist set covers the shared-vs-local split, and it applies to Cursor, Claude Code, and Conductor alike.

ideas.rule: When a settings file is relocated to a new harness-owned path, every key from the old file must be accounted for in the new one — carried over, or the change must say why it was dropped.
ideas.why: Config relocations are reviewed as renames and the diff hides dropped keys: the deleted file and the added file are separate hunks, so a reviewer never sees them side by side. A check that diffs the key sets across a delete+add pair would catch silent capability loss. This PR also quietly rewrote the `archive` command's Node flag (`--no-warnings=` to `--disable-warning=`) while relocating it, which is exactly the kind of change a rename-shaped diff conceals.

ideas.rule: A harness settings or environment file must not hardcode a model identifier inside a command string; it should read from a shared default (env var, config constant) so the setting cannot silently pin the whole team to a retired model.
ideas.why: `other-checklist.md` is a stub, so nothing today catches a committed harness config that embeds a vendor-specific model name. The failure is silent — the entry keeps running against a stale or decommissioned model and nobody notices until results drift. It is mechanically checkable (does a command string in a settings file match a known model-id pattern?) and applies to any repo whose harness config invokes an LLM.

ideas.rule: Every runnable entry a harness settings file exposes to an agent or a one-click UI must carry a human-readable description of what it does and whether it has side effects — an icon and a command string are not enough to judge whether running it is safe.
ideas.why: The stub `other-checklist.md` has no notion of documenting exposed actions. A settings file that surfaces run buttons to both humans and agents is a launch surface, and an undescribed entry invites an agent to invoke a long-running, costly, or destructive command by name-matching alone. Generalizes to `.cursor/environment.json`, `.codex/config.toml`, and any harness that maps labels to shell commands.

ideas.rule: A harness environment/settings file that defines a `start` (or equivalent boot) command must not discard the command's output — silencing stdout and stderr makes a failed agent environment indistinguishable from a healthy one.
ideas.why: other-checklist.md is a stub, so nothing today catches a boot command that fails silently. `"start": "sudo dockerd >/dev/null 2>&1 &"` backgrounds the daemon and throws away every diagnostic, so an agent whose docker-compose dependencies never came up reports only downstream errors. This is mechanically detectable (redirection to /dev/null in a start/setup/install key) and would fire in any repo using Cursor environment.json, devcontainer.json, or Codex setup scripts.

ideas.rule: A harness environment file that grants elevated privileges (passwordless sudo, root, or docker-group membership) should state why the elevation is needed, since the file is the agent's whole permission surface.
ideas.why: other-checklist.md has a TODO for exactly 'minimal permission scope' and 'change rationale' but no check. This PR gives the agent user unrestricted NOPASSWD sudo and docker-group access, and the JSON carries no rationale — only the Dockerfile comment does, and the Dockerfile is not part of the harness config an auditor reads. A generalizable check would require elevation in a settings/env artifact to be accompanied by a stated justification.
